opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's surprisingly hard to measure, and the benchmarks we have tend to tell a more optimistic story than what you see when you look closely at real engineering work.

If you look at something like SWE-bench, where models resolve real GitHub issues, progress has been really fast. A couple of years ago models were solving a few percent of those tasks, and now the best systems solve a large majority. On competitive programming, models are at or near the level of very strong human competitors. So on narrow, well-specified tasks with a clear success criterion, they're already quite impressive.

But what a top software engineer does is quite different from solving a self-contained issue with unit tests attached. A lot of the value comes from working over long horizons: understanding a large, messy codebase, figuring out what the actual problem is when it's poorly specified, making architectural decisions whose consequences only show up weeks later, coordinating with other people, and noticing when the whole approach is wrong. Benchmarks mostly don't capture that, partly because those things are expensive to evaluate, and partly because anything you can cleanly score tends to be the kind of thing models get good at first.

So the way I'd assess it is to look at a few signals together. One is task length: how long a task, measured in how long it takes a skilled human, can a model complete reliably? That has been growing quite steadily, roughly doubling every several months, which is a useful trend to extrapolate from, with caveats. Another is reliability: getting something right one time in five versus nineteen times out of twenty is a huge difference for whether you can actually delegate work. And a third is real-world uptake: are companies actually handing larger chunks of engineering to these systems, and is productivity measurably changing? That's messier data, but it's ultimately what matters.

Putting that together, my view is that we're well past "autocomplete" and into systems that can do meaningful junior-to-mid-level chunks of work under supervision, but there's still a real gap to the best engineers, mostly in long-horizon judgment and autonomy rather than raw coding ability. The interesting question is how quickly that gap closes, and given how fast the task-horizon trend has moved, I don't think it's safe to assume it'll take very long.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI systems as useful for meaningful engineering work under supervision, while saying they still fall short of the best engineers in judgment and autonomy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I like to think about this is in terms of task length and task complexity, rather than just asking "is it as good as a top engineer" in some binary sense. At Epoch and in the work we've done with METR and others, one of the clearest trends we've seen is that the length of software tasks that models can complete autonomously, measured by how long it would take a skilled human to do them, has been doubling roughly every seven months or so, and if anything that's accelerated over the last couple of years. So a few years ago you had models that could reliably do things that take a human a few minutes. Now you have systems that can do tasks that take a competent engineer several hours, sometimes a full day, with a reasonable success rate.

That said, I'd be careful about over-reading that. Benchmarks like SWE-bench and the like are measuring fairly well-scoped problems: here's a repository, here's an issue, produce a patch that passes the tests. That's a real and important chunk of what engineers do, but top software engineers aren't valuable primarily because they can close well-specified tickets. They're valuable because they figure out what the ticket should be, they understand a large messy codebase that's accumulated years of context, they make architectural decisions that only pay off months later, and they coordinate with other people. On those dimensions, the systems are still noticeably weaker. They struggle with very long-horizon context, they can be overconfident, and they don't accumulate on-the-job understanding the way a person who's been on a team for three years does.

So my assessment is something like: on the narrow, measurable slice of the job, models have gone from clearly below a junior engineer to somewhere in the range of a solid mid-level engineer, and on some sub-tasks, like writing a well-specified function quickly or finding a bug in a given file, they're already faster than almost any human. But the frontier of "top engineer" keeps receding as we discover which parts of the job are actually hard. I think the honest thing to say is that the gap is closing much faster than most people expected five years ago, and that the remaining gap is mostly about autonomy over long horizons rather than raw coding ability. And if the task-length trend holds, that gap could close within a handful of years, which has pretty big implications, because software engineering is both a huge economic sector and the input to AI research itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes models as capable of completing useful coding subtasks, sometimes faster than humans, while noting they remain weaker at long-horizon context, architectural decisions, and coordination that top engineers handle. This distinguishes task-level usefulness from replacing the full role.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve seen substantial progress, but there’s an important distinction between solving a well-specified programming problem and doing the full job of a top software engineer. That job involves figuring out what to build, understanding a large codebase, making architectural decisions, and checking that a change actually solves the underlying problem.

AI systems are increasingly capable at individual pieces of that work. The harder question is how reliably they can put those pieces together over a long task, especially when the requirements are ambiguous or feedback is incomplete. A system can produce an impressive solution in one interaction and still need considerable supervision across an entire project.

So I would look at the length and complexity of tasks these systems can complete independently, and how much human intervention they require. Consistently handling substantial engineering projects with little oversight would be much stronger evidence of reaching the abilities of top engineers than performance on short coding problems alone.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes AI’s growing usefulness on individual engineering tasks from independently doing the full job of a top software engineer, which still requires broad project work and little oversight.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve seen very substantial progress, but there’s still a gap between doing well on a coding benchmark and being a top software engineer. These systems are increasingly good at solving well-specified problems: you give them a task, a codebase, and some way to check whether the solution works. They’re less reliable when they have to figure out what the task should be, understand a large system, and carry out a project over a long period of time.

A top engineer does much more than write code. They make architectural decisions, identify requirements that weren’t explicitly stated, and notice when they’re solving the wrong problem. So I’d look at how long and how independently an AI can work on a realistic project, and how much human intervention it needs. Progress on that seems quite rapid, but I wouldn’t equate strong performance on individual coding tasks with having the full abilities of a top engineer.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes strong performance on coding tasks from possessing a top engineer’s full abilities, but it does not clearly say that AI systems are useful to top software engineers.
